articles.title: Hasan Piker complains the far left has less leverage with Democratic Party because the Dems won too many seats
articles.summary: Hasan Piker lamented Democrats' vast midterm margin weakened the far left's leverage, saying a smaller win could have allowed socialists to pressure the part...
articles.body:
Far-left streamer Hasan Piker lamented that Democrats were so successful in the midterms they aren't as dependent on their far-left flank.

The Democrats won a resounding victory in the midterms, which surprised not only the Republican Party, but the far left. Just a month before the midterms, Piker had talked about using the far left to pressure candidate James Talarico to push progressive policy, saying, "We are the force that allowed him to win this seat of power, and if he wants to maintain it, he's got to play ball."

On Wednesday night, however, Piker played a different tune, noting that the Democratic Party was so successful it is no longer as dependent on support from its most left-wing members.

"I think that there was a way that we could possibly get out of this fight with clear concessions on our agenda. We didn't. Part of that was because nobody expected the margin to be so vast," he said.

"If the margin was 10, then we could have made an impact. If the Democratic Party's margin of victory was 10 and not like f---ing 40, OK, then yeah, we could have had a big caucus, a socialist caucus, a fighter caucus, whatever you want to call it, that could potentially bully the party to be more responsive to the needs of the masses."

Piker also hit back at some critical comments from his fans.

"'This is you at your worst,'" he read aloud one comment before responding. "Why? Because I have to explain to you as an adult who is a political pundit how, you know, how change never really happens in Washington, D.C.?

"It hurts your feelings to hear someone explain to you why these things happen while simultaneously telling you how much I oppose it? Does it hurt your feelings to hear how this goes?" he asked. "It's just reality.

"I'm going to continue to explain how the sausage gets made, even if that hurts your f---ing feelings, because you're too dumb to understand."

Republican consultant Mary Marslender reacted to Piker's commentary.

"Hasan Piker is furious that Democrats won too many seats because it weakened the (Democratic Socialists of America's) ability to hold the Democratic Party hostage. Piker's complaint reveals that the far left prefers narrow majorities so it can force its destructive socialist experiments on our country and European-style street chaos," she told Fox News Digital.

Democratic strategist and co-host of "The Huddle" podcast Dan Turrentine told Fox News Digital, "There is the world as Hasan Piker wished it would be, and the real world. Socialists are utterly irrelevant in the next Congress. They are not the majority of America, nor are they the majority of the Democratic Party.

"In fact, in the next Congress, socialists will be a tiny 2.7% of the House Democratic caucus and there will be only one in the Senate, Bernie Sanders."

images.caption: Livestreamer Hasan Piker had previously talked about potentially using the far left's leverage to push Texas Democrat James Talarico to govern with a left-wing agenda.
Far-left pundit Hasan Piker berated his listeners, saying that this latest bad news can be understood with a basic grasp of politics.

articles.title: The last big midterms mystery: Who will these future governors choose to replace them in the Senate?
articles.summary: Minnesota's Amy Klobuchar and Tennessee's Marsha Blackburn will have the power to personally select their successors when they're sworn in to their states' t...
articles.body:
The last undecided Senate race finally got a winner on Tuesday night when Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan to give her party its ninth flipped seat this midterm cycle.

Peltola's win, which came more than two weeks after Election Day, means the final balance of power in the Senate is set. When the new Congress convenes for the first time in January, Democrats will control 56 seats, and Republicans will hold 44 seats.

But there are still two important questions that remain unanswered about the next Senate caucus. As it stands, we only know the identities of 98 of the 100 senators who will serve in the upcoming Congress, and it could be weeks before we find out who those last two pivotal lawmakers will be.

That's because two current senators, Tennessee Republican Marsha Blackburn and Minnesota Democrat Amy Klobuchar, were each elected governor of their home states. They will need to leave the Senate to assume their new positions.

Laws in Tennessee and Minnesota give governors the power to temporarily fill Senate vacancies. That means Blackburn and Klobuchar can each choose their own successor as one of their first acts as governor if they wait to resign from the Senate until shortly before they're sworn in. Both have indicated they plan to do so but have offered very few clues about who they might consider.

It's highly unlikely that either of them would select a replacement from the opposition party, so the partisan split in the Senate probably won't change. But their decisions will still carry a lot of weight. Whoever they choose will occupy two of the most important legislative seats in the U.S. government and could play a significant role in defining the ideological direction of their respective parties.

Blackburn, who has represented Tennessee in the Senate since 2019, announced her bid for governor in August 2025, just nine months after winning reelection to a second Senate term. This year's gubernatorial race was much closer than Republicans in the Volunteer State are accustomed to, but Blackburn was still able to defeat her Democratic challenger, Jerri Green, by more than 50,000 votes. She is the first woman elected to the state's top office.

Blackburn is a staunch conservative and Trump ally. She opened her first gubernatorial campaign video by saying, "Trump is back. America is blessed and Tennessee: better than ever." Her MAGA credentials suggest she's likely to select a successor with a similar profile, but that won't be certain until her choice is formally announced.

Throughout the campaign, Blackburn repeatedly declined to answer questions about who she might choose to replace her but said early on in the process that she intended to make the decision herself, rather than leaving it up to outgoing Republican Gov. Bill Lee.

That hadn't changed in the weeks since she was formally elected. She told Fox News on Nov. 15 that she hadn't made up her mind and didn't yet have a "short list" of potential replacements.

"I'm focused on finishing the work in the Senate and transitioning to governor," she said.

Blackburn's coyness hasn't stopped speculation about who her selection might be. In the days after Democrats' decisive midterm performance earlier this month — which many top Republicans attributed to voters' dissatisfaction with the war in Iran — rumors began to spread that Blackburn might choose embattled Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to fill her seat. Those rumors were quickly refuted by sources close to Blackburn.

The two names that have been most frequently suggested as Blackburn's replacement are former Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs and U.S. Rep. Tim Burchett.

Jacobs turned to politics after a long career in professional wrestling, where he performed as the horror-themed character Kane. He told Fox News in September that it would be a "huge honor" to be Blackburn's chosen successor and he would "consider it very seriously" if asked.

Burchett, who represents Tennessee's deep red Second District in the House of Representatives, has said he "absolutely" wants to be considered for the position. He has also made clear that he intends to run for the Senate in 2028 against Blackburn's pick if she chooses someone other than him.

Blackburn is scheduled to be sworn in as governor on Jan. 16 and would likely appoint her replacement shortly after taking office. Whoever she chooses will hold her seat until the 2028 general election, when a special election will be held to decide who will finish out the remaining two years of her term.

When Minnesota's Democratic Gov. Tim Walz abruptly dropped his bid for a third term in January, reports immediately began to circulate that Klobuchar was considering launching a bid to replace him. She made it official a few weeks later. A former presidential candidate with a strong record of success in statewide races, Klobuchar quickly became the frontrunner in the Minnesota governor's race. She easily defeated Republican Lisa Demuth on Election Day. She will be the first woman to serve as governor of her state as well when she's sworn in on Jan. 4.

Like Blackburn, Klobuchar has said she intends to choose her own successor and has remained mum on who she may be considering. One name that can be crossed off the list is Walz, who said he would "rather eat glass" than take over her Senate seat.

Under Minnesota law, Klobuchar's successor would fill her seat on a temporary basis until November 2027, when a special election will be held to decide who will finish the remaining three years of her term. Because of that short time frame, Klobuchar has described the appointment as an "interim position."

"It would be for about a year," she told a local news station last month.

Nothing in Minnesota law bars appointees from running to keep their seat, but there is some recent history of governors filling vacancies with lawmakers who promise not to campaign for reelection.

Replacements often end up holding on to their seats, however. Minnesota's other senator, Tina Smith, was appointed to her seat in 2018 and has been reelected twice since then. Smith is retiring when her term ends in January.

Klobuchar could insist that her successor pledge to serve only as a temporary placeholder, but she hasn't said whether she might disqualify potential candidates who decline to do so.

Her selection, and the Senate race that will follow in November, could say a lot about the ideological direction of the Democratic Party. Midwest swing states were home to some of the most tightly contested midterm primary battles between progressive and moderate candidates anywhere in the country.

Minnesota's Senate primary was won by the more left-leaning candidate, Peggy Flanagan. The same thing happened in nearby Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed eked out a primary win over moderate Haley Stevens. Both Flanagan and El-Sayed won their general election races earlier this month.

articles.title: Mulheres respondem por mais de 11 mil negócios em Presidente Prudente | G1
articles.standfirst: Mulheres representam 47% do total de empreendedores na capital do oeste paulista. Em todo o estado de São Paulo, são 2,5 milhões de donas de negócios, segundo levantamento do Sebrae.
articles.summary: O número de mulheres a frente de negócios representa 47% do total de empreendedores em Presidente Prudente (SP); são 11 mil mulheres, do total de quase 25 mil atuando no ramo.
articles.body:
O número de mulheres a frente de negócios representa 47% do total de empreendedores em Presidente Prudente (SP): são 11 mil mulheres atuando no ramo. No estado de São Paula, são 2,5 milhões de empreendedoras femininas.

Da quantidade total de moradores que atuam como empreendedores na capital do oeste paulista, são quase 25 mil empreendedores. Em Bauru, tem o dobro de pessoas empreendendo e também cerca de 46% são mulheres à frente dos negócios.

A atuação é principalmente em áreas de beleza e varejo, como cabelereira e venda de roupas e acessórios. São as atividades econômicas mais procuradas pelas mulheres empreendedoras em Prudente, além da confeitaria, como o caso de Camila Carrara, que trocou de carreira há 10 anos para conseguir cuidar da filha.

“Valeu muito a pena [trocar de área]. Todo início tem os seus desafios, mas a gente precisa ter paciência e persistência. Precisei desenvolver várias habilidades que eu não tinha”, descreve, à TV TEM.

Presidente Prudente soma mais de 11 mil mulheres à frente de negócios: confeitaria e beleza são as áreas mais procuradas — Foto: Reprodução/TV TEM

Para ajudar na capacitação, Camila afirma que se dedicou a diversos cursos que ajudassem no negócio. “Vale muito a pena fazer o que a gente ama”, destaca a confeiteira.

A analista de negócios do Sebrae de Presidente Prudente, Ana Camile Pena, cita exemplos dos quais as mulheres são responsáveis pelo sustento de toda a família.

“Elas precisam complementar a renda. Elas percebem que podem melhorar a qualidade de vida e dos filhos, então por isso essa procura tem aumentado cada vez mais”, explica a analista.

Para ajudar, o Sebrae oferece um programa específico, voltado ao desenvolvimento para estimular o empreendedorismo feminino.

“O programa vai atrelar ações como cursos, capacitações, tanto em qualificação profissional para ajudar essa pessoa a conquistar uma nova renda, quanto também em gestão”, reforça a analista.

articles.title: The GOP's unlikely new duo on Capitol Hill
articles.summary: John Thune and Jim Jordan barely know each other despite spending 20 years together in Congress. Now they have to get to work.
articles.body:
The future of the Republican Party on Capitol Hill is in the hands of a real odd couple.

One is a lanky ex-basketball star, the other a compact former wrestling champion. One is a courtly practitioner of old-school GOP politics, the other a symbol of hard-line MAGA confrontation. One is viewed with suspicion by the party's conservative base, the other is seen as an icon.

And despite nearly 50 years of congressional service between them, John Thune and Jim Jordan barely know each other. Now as their party's top Senate and House leaders, respectively, they have to find a way to work together if Republicans want to spend the next two years fighting Democrats and not each other.

Their first one-on-one meeting following the massive GOP losses earlier this month was mainly a get-to-know-you session. According to Jordan, they talked about sports, lamented their shared history of knee problems and compared their number of children and grandchildren — four and nine for Jordan, 62; two and six for Thune, 65.

But come January, the two men will have to get down to business. They now have a shared responsibility to shape their party's message as they try to define the huge new Democratic majorities and start to claw their way back to power.

"We got to focus on who we are as Republicans, what our party is about, how we're going to help families," Jordan said in an interview, adding that "the House and Senate are different, but we're Republicans."

Answering those questions about the GOP hasn't been simple under President Donald Trump, but both leaders are betting — or at least hoping — that being out of power will focus Republicans and tamp down the frequent squabbling between chambers.

Jordan and Thune, who previously served in the House, know they are each operating in what can often seem like parallel universes and are so far being respectful of each other's institutional realities.

Thune called Jordan a "team player" who wants to "keep Republicans from fighting Republicans" — a far cry from the "legislative terrorist" moniker bestowed on the Ohioan by former Speaker John Boehner in Jordan's past life as an anti-leadership gadfly.

"I think that's a good quality in the work that we have to do, especially now," the South Dakotan said.

Inside the Capitol, the two men are both polite midwesterners who are comfortable slapping colleagues' backs and toeing the party line with reporters. Both are quietly observant Christians, devoted family men and former college athletes who spend a lot of time in the gym.

But some of their colleagues said in interviews they see some clear lines of delineation given their respective strengths and weaknesses.

As those Republicans view it, Jordan, a regular on the cable news networks, will be a front-facing media messenger, reflecting his popularity among GOP voters. Thune, whose standing with the MAGA base has deteriorated over the past year, is a strong fundraiser, remains well-liked among his colleagues and can work effectively behind closed doors.

"Jordan is going to be the fighter, and Thune will probably be very behind-the-scenes," said one GOP senator who was granted anonymity to speak candidly.

Jordan and Thune face wildly different challenges in maintaining party discipline next year. In the House, Democrats would have to lose scores of their own members before they would need help from Republicans to pass bills. But in the Senate, Thune is at risk of just four GOP members peeling off to join Democrats and advance legislation — especially early in the year when the new majority is expected to move bills specifically designed to split Republicans.

There are already signs Jordan could come under pressure from his ideological home base — members of the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus — to battle Thune and the Senate GOP writ large when necessary.

Rep. Eric Burlison (R-Mo.), a possible chair of the Freedom Caucus next year, said he understood Jordan and Thune might "be friends at first" in the minority "because, why not?" But he said he hoped the two leaders can ultimately "be blunt and honest with each other and fight."

"At the end of the day, I want to see a [leader] that's going to fight for the House and not defend the Senate," Burlison said. "That's the one thing I wish that we had — that our leadership had put the Senate on the spot harder."

In his former incarnation as a Freedom Caucus co-founder and hard-right sparkplug, Jordan was among those taking shots at Senate Republicans. During President Joe Biden's presidency, for instance, he attacked GOP senators who voted to advance bipartisan deals on gun control and infrastructure.

More recently, he's kept his fire trained outside the party tent. But many House Republicans spent the last two years publicly criticizing Thune for the Senate's inability to overcome Democratic filibusters and move top GOP priorities.

They include the outgoing speaker, Mike Johnson , whose penchant for shifting blame to the Senate — or, in the views of some Thune allies, misrepresenting private conversations with his counterpart across the Capitol — added unnecessary friction into the interchamber relationship.

Thune typically avoids giving Johnson public advice or advising the House on what to do, a courtesy those Thune allies don't believe Johnson — who frequently notes he can't control the Senate — has reciprocated.

The two men, despite being close in age, have taken different paths to power. Thune climbed up the Senate GOP leadership ladder before becoming top leader in 2025. He also previously served as chair of the Senate Commerce Committee and as a member of the similarly wonky Finance Committee.

Jordan, on the other hand, is entering leadership for the first time in January after two previous failed attempts. Jordan has led Republicans on the Oversight and Judiciary committees — panels that tend to be more focused on investigations and messaging than hardcore policymaking.

Though Thune got his start in the House, only eight members he served with during his three terms in the chamber will still be there next year. Jordan, meanwhile, has some established relationships with Republicans in the Senate — particularly with Rick Scott of Florida and Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, who have clashed with Thune at times.

Scott, who lost a 2024 leadership challenge to Thune, described Jordan in an interview as "easy to work with" and a "positive influence.""I think they'll work well together," he added.

North Dakota Sen. Kevin Cramer , a former House Republican who served with Jordan and had dinner with him this week, said in an interview that the Ohioan will "do what he's supposed to do" and "has a respect" for his soon-to-be counterpart.

"People should not confuse personal relationships with outward rhetoric in this arena," Cramer said. "There's mutual respect in the battle and an understandable competitiveness, but at the end of the day, we're just people trying to get a job done."

articles.title: Christian nationalists see Republicans' midterm losses as an opportunity to supplant Trump's MAGA
articles.summary: IRVING, Texas (AP) — Christian nationalists once celebrated President Donald Trump’s return to the White House as a victory for their movement. Now they see...
articles.body:
IRVING, Texas (AP) — Christian nationalists once celebrated President Donald Trump's return to the White House as a victory for their movement. Now they see the Republican Party's recent election losses as an opportunity to supplant his "Make America Great Again" movement with their extremist vision.

Many gathered in Texas last week for a three-day conference where Nick Fuentes , an avowed white nationalist, was the surprise special guest. The way he sees it, the midterms effectively dethroned Trump as the party's leader.

"This is like the death of Josef Stalin," Fuentes said, his high-register voice reverberating in a dark and cavernous convention hall. "And there is nothing that will fill the void right now."

But that's exactly what Joel Webbon wants to do.

A 40-year-old pastor and podcaster with a precisely sculpted salt and pepper beard, Webbon organized the conference, "Christ is King: America After Trump," and served as its master of ceremonies.

Goal of increasing the clout of Christian nationalism

Webbon's movement, which seeks a theocratic government and patriarchal society, remains on the political fringe, and there were no elected officials on stage. Webbon said conservative leaders won't give him the time of day "because they want their base to not even know I exist."

As rival factions wrestle over the Republicans' future, Webbon is planning to expand the influence of Christian nationalism. The conference, where organizers said more than 1,000 people attended, was a start as the movement looks toward Washington.

"We can clearly say they have been gaining power," said Julie Ingersoll, a professor of religious studies at University of North Florida who has focused on Christian nationalism. "I wouldn't dismiss them."

In Webbon's vision, the United States is largely made up of white Christians, the Apostles' Creed is the preamble to the U.S. Constitution, at least 50 million people are deported, interracial marriage is considered "not normal," and Jews, Muslims, Hindus and women don't have the right to vote or hold public office.

While Webbon doesn't expect that to come to fruition anytime soon, he and his allies hope the Election Day shattering of Trump's coalition will allow them to pick up the pieces and start down that road.

"Phase one is kind of complete," Webbon said on stage.

A girl in the third row kicked her yellow shoes that didn't reach the floor. Young men, several wearing blue "America First" caps sold by Fuentes, listened attentively.

"We're moving into phase two," Webbon said. "It's time to get the numbers. It's time to get the donors. It's time to get our guys into positions of power."

Disappointment with Trump was widespread

Right-wing Christians have long been some of Trump's most dedicated supporters. Although Trump never had a reputation as religious, they viewed him as a political battering ram against their cultural opponents, and he positioned himself as a defender of evangelical values.

Christian nationalism goes a step further.

"This isn't your next-door neighbor's Christianity," Ingersoll said. "They want America to be a Christian nation in a very specific kind of way. And that's going to be exclusively for Christians, mostly for white Christians."

Trump's choice of Pete Hegseth as defense secretary was viewed as progress for the movement. Hegseth belongs to a church network co-founded by a Christian nationalist pastor, and he reposted a video last year that included arguments that women shouldn't be allowed to vote.

Trump dined with Fuentes at the president's Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida in between his two White House terms and has repeatedly declined to denounce Fuentes.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment for this story.

There was little goodwill toward the president at the "Christ is King" conference. One of the more charitable assessments from speakers was that Trump imperiled the Republican project enough to allow an opening.

"Did anybody get fooled with Trump?" asked JP Sears, a right-wing YouTube comedian.

"Boy, he was good, he was, I fell for that," Sears said. "'He's going to dismantle the deep state, he is going to root out the corruption in the system.' And here we are, he is the corruption."

After Sears spoke, attendees heard from one of the conference's sponsors, a wealth manager, and then checked out the booths in a hall adjacent to the stage.

There was a stand selling T-shirts saying "I'll take the Christian, hold the Judeo." People stood on vibrating platforms that proclaimed the benefits of lymphatic drainage and stress reduction. Children's books focused on the foibles of socialism.

Kyle Fischer, a 34-year-old volunteer, was selling Webbon's book, "White Genocide." Fischer said American Jews should leave for Israel. "Go. You have your nation. This is ours," he said.

"Do I want them dead or anything? No. Come to Christ. You're my brother," he said, adding later, "call me antisemitic, call me a Nazi, I don't care anymore."

Some Republicans, notably Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, have warned about growing antisemitism on the political right. Even some attendees seemed uncomfortable with how Webbon and his allies talked about different races not being compatible or equal.

Webbon, who has almost 140,000 followers on X, said his worldview prioritizes religion over race, whereas white nationalists do the opposite or eschew religion altogether. The distinction makes little difference to people who study his movement.

"So it doesn't have to just be white folk," said Michael Emerson, a Rice University professor of sociology who has focused on ideologies around religion and race. "But you've got to support ultimately that white folks are in the dominant."

Webbon doesn't expect attendees to agree with him on everything, and he's looking for any chance to pull people into his ideological orbit.

Seth Goforth, a 19-year-old from Memphis, Tennessee, said he started listening to Webbon a year ago and initially thought he seemed racist. Goforth eventually saw Webbon as focusing more on "heritage and culture," and was drawn in.

Micah Murphy, Goforth's 18-year-old friend, had a similar view. Webbon "is a little bit on the edgier side" on race, Murphy said, but "I haven't yet heard him say anything that contradicts Scripture."

Christian nationalists are ready for the next phase

Webbon said phase one of his plan was achieved in the midterm wipeout for Republicans.

Phase two is expanding the political machinery, such as door-knockers, campaign donors and phone banks. Phase three is winning elected office, "ideally the presidency," Webbon said in an interview, but at least "we need a couple governors or some Senate races."

Then there's phase four, which is "to get the rest of our guys into serious positions of influence."

Webbon knows his politics are unsavory to the broader American public, and so does Fuentes, but both said they are having discussions with people thinking of running for president. They wouldn't name the possible candidates, recognizing that their association could be a liability.

But Webbon thinks the limits of what's acceptable will shift. Right now, he said, the goal is to "break containment."

articles.title: Voters oust some sheriffs who signed pacts to help Trump's immigration enforcement efforts
articles.summary: (AP) — As he ran for sheriff in North Carolina against a longtime incumbent who had joined forces with the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, Shan...
articles.body:
GRAHAM, N.C. (AP) — As he ran for sheriff in North Carolina against a longtime incumbent who had joined forces with the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, Shannon Long found his campaign van was an obstacle with some voters.

The trust between law enforcement and Alamance County's growing Latino community was so fractured, Long said, that the vehicle emblazoned with "sheriff" made it a struggle to get some people to speak with him.

"They've been living in fear. They feel like they don't have a voice. They have been suppressed, oppressed; a lot of them are depressed. So they feel that they live in a community where they don't belong," Long, a pastor, business owner and former sheriff's deputy, told The Associated Press two weeks after defeating Republican Sheriff Terry Johnson in a campaign that some activists, voters and local officials say turned partly on questions about immigration enforcement and the treatment of Latino residents.

Johnson is one of a few sheriffs around the country who were ousted by challengers critical of their cooperation with President Donald Trump's push for mass deportations of people in the country illegally. While only a smattering, the results could spell trouble for other sheriffs who are seen as participants in Trump's crackdown and possibly hinder agreements that have become a cornerstone of the administration's efforts.

Johnson was among the first sheriffs to allow his deputies to enforce federal immigration laws under what's known as a 287(g) agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Long, who ran as an independent, promised to curtail cooperation with ICE, which continues to rely on the cooperative pacts to boost arrest numbers despite a one-time infusion of $75 billion from Congress and hiring about 12,000 officers .

The administration has more than 2,700 such pacts with state and local agencies, up from 135 when Trump began his second term. The agreements, predominantly in the South, have deputized over 29,000 local law officers and resulted in more than 6,600 arrests in July, about 15% of all ICE arrests, according to government data obtained by the Deportation Data Project that was analyzed by the advocacy group fwd.us .

The AP reviewed about 250 elections held this month for sheriffs whose offices had 287(g) agreements, identifying races in Indiana, Maryland, North Carolina, Wisconsin and elsewhere in which ICE pacts played a role in a candidate's defeat. Many sheriffs who ran this year were unopposed. But the ICE agreements could become a focus again in two years, when sheriffs from Florida, Texas and other states with large numbers of 287(g) agreements are up for election.

A new sheriff is coming to 'No Chance Alamance'

Alamance County is a longtime Republican stronghold of just under 200,000 residents that sits between Greensboro and the Research Triangle metropolitan area that includes Raleigh, Durham and Chapel Hill. It has become more politically competitive as its population has grown increasingly diverse — from 750 residents who identified as Hispanic in the 1990 census to nearly 25,000 in 2020. The sheriff's office currently participates in the 287(g) program, a spokesman confirmed, though last year it ended an agreement to house ICE detainees.

Johnson, who is white, was first elected in 2002 and has been a prominent and polarizing figure. He has insisted he welcomes lawful immigrants and denied persistent allegations — including in a Justice Department lawsuit over a decade ago that ended with a settlement — that his office racially profiled minority residents.

The county acquired the moniker "No Chance Alamance" because of a perceived sense of unjust policing and a lack of political representation among Black and Latino residents, school board member Seneca Rogers said.

Johnson initially said in a phone call that immigration policy could have contributed to his loss. But in a brief interview later, he said it likely didn't and laid blame with his long tenure and a national political environment that was brutal for Republicans , acutely so in North Carolina , where Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper flipped a U.S. Senate seat, winning by nearly 20 percentage points. He said he always followed the law and protected public safety.

Activists and longtime residents said the Latino community — and to some extent, the Black community — feared engaging with the sheriff's office and described a sense that non-white residents were far likelier to be pulled over or detained after a traffic stop. Some people were afraid to call 911 or even go to work, said community organizer Leslie Arevalo.

Voter Renee Russell said the sheriff's cooperation with ICE gave a false impression of Alamance as unwelcoming. She was excited to see fresh leadership. Long will be the county's first Black sheriff, local media reported.

But Republican state Sen. Amy Galey, whose district includes the county, defended Johnson's record. She said he had worked to improve training opportunities and mental health services. Although Galey didn't think immigration played a big role in the race, she wondered if hard-line ICE tactics elsewhere could have contributed to simmering concerns about law enforcement more broadly.

The sheriff's office in Frederick County, Maryland, northwest of Washington, D.C., was another longtime participant in the 287(g) program. Since 2008, the county detained and turned over 1,884 people to ICE, Republican Sheriff Chuck Jenkins said. But that came to a halt this year when Democratic Gov. Wes Moore signed a law banning immigration enforcement pacts with the federal government.

Public sentiment also turned against Jenkins, who said the program made the community safer but acknowledged it likely cost him reelection. He was defeated by Democrat Karl Bickel, a retired U.S. Department of Justice employee who had lost four previous elections to Jenkins and pledged not to cooperate with ICE.

"In general, people are fed up with the sheriff's negativeness about immigrants," said retired social worker Carol Antoniewicz, who distributed emails, social media posts and campaign literature in support of Bickel.

In Wisconsin's Winnebago County, ICE's arrest and detention of a schoolteacher weeks before Election Day sparked backlash against anyone seemingly supportive of immigration officers, including a Republican vying to replace a retiring sheriff.

"Any kind of perceived alignment definitely is considered a liability at this point," said Molly Smiltneek, a local advocate and immigration lawyer who attended a vigil for the teacher.

Though the sheriff's department had nothing to do with the teacher's arrest, its 287(g) agreement became central to the campaign, boosting Democrat Jason Rippl, who promised to end it.

A newly elected sheriff seeks a better community partnership

Long, who formerly worked as a deputy in a neighboring North Carolina county, said he will uphold the law in his new role and hold offenders accountable. But he said he won't participate in the 287(g) program.

He has set up meetings with the Latino community in the hopes of building new relationships.

"I want them to see the sheriff's office in the community, creating a partnership, letting them know that they have a voice. … There's no need to operate in fear," he said.

Schuettler reported from Phoenix and Lieb from Jefferson City, Missouri. Associated Press journalist Allen G. Breed contributed from Graham.

articles.title: Republicans seeking an alternative to JD Vance ask: How about a governor?
articles.summary: Several current and former GOP governors are either keeping the door open to running or pushing for one of their own to be the nominee.
articles.body:
As Republicans weigh alternatives to Vice President JD Vance for president in 2028, at least one question has increasingly bubbled up since the midterms: How about a governor?

Several current and former GOP governors are either keeping the door open to running or pushing for one of their own to be the nominee. The discussion shows how Republicans see room to maneuver around Vance after their party's devastating midterm losses.

At least four current or former GOP governors are signaling their national ambitions: Govs. Ron DeSantis of Florida, Brian Kemp of Georgia and Sarah Huckabee Sanders of Arkansas, as well as former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin. And at least two others – Govs. Spencer Cox of Utah and Kevin Stitt of Oklahoma – have said this year that they prefer the 2028 nominee be a governor, an implicit snub of Vance.

"In this climate, where people are ticked off at DC in general — Republican, Democrat alike — being removed from that, being able to get things done and being removed are kind of like the magic one-two punch," said former Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker, a Republican who ran for president in 2016.

Vance and his allies aren't ignoring the talk.

They launched an offensive against Stitt on Thursday after he suggested lawmakers from both parties focus on immigration reform in President Donald Trump's final two years. Vance said any effort at "amnesty" would be "morally and electorally disastrous." Stitt thanked Vance "for bringing governors into the conversation."

It's all part of the GOP's post-election reassessment of whether there is an opening for a Republican not named Vance.

"I don't think there's any doubt it's gotten wider since [Nov. 3]," said Marc Short, who was chief of staff to former Vice President Mike Pence. "I think it was such a shellacking and a rejection of the last two years that they'll have to be candidates who look and say, 'Maybe there's an opening for me.' But I still think it's a pretty narrow path."

Walker also offered a note of caution for governors, saying they cannot run alone on their statehouse records.

"You've got to translate that to, 'Look what I did, and here's what I'm going to do next,'" Walker said.

Even after the midterms, some potential 2028 candidates have acknowledged Vance would be hard to beat, especially with Trump's support. Huckabee Sanders said Friday on HBO's "Real Time with Bill Maher" that Vance is "still the most dominant figure on the Republican side … and starts with a tremendous lead."

DeSantis appeared more bearish on Vance in a New York Times interview published Friday. "VPs tend to be derivative," DeSantis said.

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who is leaving office after Trump helped defeat him in his primary, questioned in a recent interview whether Vance would remain in Trump's "good favor" ahead of 2028, noting his recent comments blaming the Iran war for the GOP's midterm losses.

"I think that's a big issue," Cornyn said. "But in 2028, I think what we'll see is, if I had to guess, I would say an outsider has a better chance than someone who's a member of the current administration, but that's two years from now."

DeSantis and Huckabee Sanders have boasted that their states withstood the "blue wave" the swept across the country. DeSantis said the day after the election that it was "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans" in other parts of the country.

"We built up a lot of trust with our voters over the years," DeSantis told CNN's Jake Tapper the same day, adding that a property tax ballot measure that he championed helped motivate an otherwise sleepy GOP base. "We were able to turn out enough voters to be able to get these guys across the finish line."

During a post-election speech to the Young America's Foundation in California, Youngkin said many voters "aren't seeing and feeling this economy that statistically is strong."

"They voted for change, and a lot of them voted for it," Youngkin said. "And so our job is not to sulk. Our job is not to make excuses. Our job is to prove with better ideas and real results that common-sense conservative policies are the surest path to the affordable, prosperous life that Americans are asking for."

Walker, who serves as president of the foundation, said Youngkin's speech was "extremely well-received."

Huckabee Sanders, who's been on a media tour promoting a new book, has said Republicans need to be more outspoken about their accomplishments and differences with Democrats.

"I don't think that our message needs to be different or needs to change," she said during a stop Tuesday at the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank in Washington, DC. "I think we just have to do a better job telling it. We have not done a great job of telling our story and talking about the things that really impact people's lives."

"That has to be a core focus moving forward as we go into the next election cycle," she added.

DeSantis, Huckabee Sanders and Youngkin have all faced questions in recent days about their interest in 2028 and not ruled it out.

The vulnerabilities governors would face

Most of the governors would have certain obvious vulnerabilities to overcome in the 2028 primary.

DeSantis and Kemp would have to overcome their past tensions with Trump. DeSantis challenged Trump in the 2024 primary, and Kemp clashed with Trump over his 2020 reelection loss in Georgia.

Both have appeared to reconcile more recently with Trump, who has made public appearances with them and complimented them.

A person familiar with Kemp's thinking said he was considering running for president but had not closed the door on other opportunities. Senate Republicans are expected to court him to challenge Georgia Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock in 2028.

One Georgia Republican strategist said Kemp would be "much different" from anti-Trump Republicans who waged longshot bids for president.

"I think the way [Kemp] dealt with Trump — he wasn't opposed to Trump, he was just doing what was best for the state," the strategist said. "Trump was mad at him at certain times, but he wasn't mad at Trump."

Youngkin and Kemp would also have to grapple with failing to keep their seats Republican after they left office. Youngkin has been clashing with his Democratic successor, Abigail Spanberger, in recent days over her decision to rescind his plan to participate in a federal school voucher program.

Kemp had an especially rough midterm cycle, endorsing candidates for Senate and governor who lost their primaries. He campaigned for the eventual nominees — Mike Collins for Senate and Rick Jackson for governor — but both lost to Democrats.

The highest-profile incoming GOP governor may be Byron Donalds in Florida. Trump endorsed him early in his campaign, and Vance campaigned with him in the final weeks of the election. Donalds said last year that Vance was the "leader in the clubhouse" for the 2028 nomination and suggested in March that he would support Vance over fellow Floridian Marco Rubio for president.

Donalds struck a different tone in a post-midterms interview.

"We'll see what happens down the line with the nomination from my party," Donalds said on NBC's "Meet the Press."

"The only thing I know is there's going to need to be a robust conversation, a robust debate."

articles.title: MAGA rep says he believes adults are ‘bad parents’ if they let their kids play the new Grand Theft Auto
articles.summary: American Psychological Association says there is not enough evidence to prove video games cause real-world violence
articles.body:
Republican Rep. Tim Burchett claimed adults who allow their children to play the long-awaited , record-breaking video game Grand Theft Auto VI are "bad parents."

The Tennessee congressman made the comments Wednesday to TMZ , one day before the game's release, arguing that its graphic depictions of crime and violence could desensitize young players. GTA VI is the franchise's first new installment in 13 years and one of the most highly anticipated video games in years.

"These kids' parents, are they wolves or something, raising their kids? I think it's really just more of a how-to video," Burchett said, comparing the game to a guide to committing crimes.

Asked whether he thought parents who let their children play the game were "bad parents," he replied, "I believe so."

Burchett also claimed that research has repeatedly linked violent video games to real-world violence, despite leading scientific organizations and research finding insufficient evidence that shows any causal link between the two.

"It desensitizes kids. They've done study after study," Burchett said. "Parents need to start raising their children."

GTA VI follows characters Jason and Lucia as they get caught up in the criminal world of Leonida, a fictional state based on Florida . Players can roam around the open-world setting, taking part in everything from car thefts and armed robberies to shootouts.

The game received an M for Mature rating from the Entertainment Software Rating Board, making it recommended for players 17 and older. The rating covers intense violence, blood and gore, nudity, sexual content, strong language, mature humor, and drug and alcohol use.

On Thursday, the White House got online backlash after posting a 30-second video of President Donald Trump edited in the style of GTA , with social media users calling the Wednesday clip "cringe" and "a little stale."

Burchett was not alone in raising concerns about the game's content. Several Fox News personalities also criticized its depictions of graphic violence and sexual material, questioning whether they could influence young players.

"Kids have these games, and what are you teaching them?" Fox News co-host Rosanna Scotto questioned during Thursday's episode of Outnumbered.

"How to steal a car, how to shoot someone, how to do something illegal. And, I don't know, does it destigmatize crime?" she said.

"My son will be nowhere near anything like this while in my household," added Kayleigh McEnany, the show's co-host and a former White House press secretary.

Fox News contributor Paul Mauro claimed: "This is almost the equivalent of giving them a gun, at an age where they don't understand responsibility."

But Florida Democratic Rep. Maxwell Frost had a different take, saying he was looking forward to playing the game and even planned to buy a PlayStation 5 just to play it.

"Look, I wasn't allowed to play GTA my entire life. I had to play The Simpsons Hit and Run … it's like GTA for kids. That's what I played. So now I have to play a lot to, you know, I have to make up for lost time," Frost told TMZ.

He also disagreed that violent video games are behind America's gun violence problem, saying parents should get to decide what games their kids can play.

"Every country has these games and has these movies. We're the only [country] that has them that actually has a real gun violence problem," he said.

Despite Burchett's claims, the connection between violent video games and real-world violence remains debated among researchers.

The American Psychological Association said in a March 2020 update that there was insufficient scientific evidence to prove violent video games cause real-world violence.

While some studies have found a small link between violent games and aggressive behavior, such as yelling or pushing, the organization cautioned against blaming video games for more serious acts of violence.

"Violence is a complex social problem that likely stems from many factors that warrant attention from researchers, policymakers and the public," APA President Sandra L. Shullman said in a statement at the time.

"Attributing violence to video gaming is not scientifically sound and draws attention away from other factors, such as a history of violence, which we know from the research is a major predictor of future violence," Shullman added.

articles.title: Former press secretary Katie Zacharia criticizes GOP over midterm losses, says party isn’t ‘good at winning’
articles.summary: Katie Zacharia, who served just five days as White House press secretary, says Republicans are "terrible at the offense" after losing nine Senate seats.
articles.body: Former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia offered a blunt assessment of her party’s midterm collapse, saying Republicans lack the offensive instincts needed to win elections. Speaking with The Free Press, Zacharia — who served as press secretary for just five days in October — weighed in on what she believes led to Democrats’ historic midterm sweep earlier this month. "There’s nobody persuasive in the Democrats, but they’ve always banked on Trump Derangement Syndrome," Zacharia told the outlet. VOTERS WANT TO 'MOVE ON' FROM THE PRESIDENT, FORMER TRUMP OFFICIAL CLAIMS AS REASON FOR GOP'S MIDTERM DEFEAT She then took aim at her own party as she looked to cast blame for Republicans losing nine Senate seats and at least 50 seats in the House of Representatives to Democratic challengers. "The Republicans are terrible at the offense," she added. "I mean, we can’t win. We’re not good at winning." LEAVITT REVEALS WHAT REPUBLICANS MUST DO TO SURVIVE POLITICALLY AFTER TRUMP LEAVES WHITE HOUSE However, Zacharia appeared to not harbor any ill-will toward her former boss, telling The Free Press that she does not intend to spill any secrets about the White House because "there’s nothing terrible to write." "President Trump made me famous," Zacharia said, boasting about her relationship with Trump. "I can’t even keep up. I had to hire someone to go track all my opportunities." WHITE HOUSE REPORTERS REACT TO KATIE ZACHARIA'S 'BRUTAL' EXIT AS TRUMP'S PRESS SECRETARY Zacharia departed her position after Trump revealed to reporters that he told her, "You don't have to do this if you don't want to. I think you should reconsider." She left the role after a rocky showing before the White House press corps and several controversies over her legal credentials after she took office. LEAVITT OPENS UP ON HELPING TRUMP FIND NEW PRESS SECRETARY AFTER ZACHARIA DEBACLE: 'WAS NOT FOR HER' Despite her short tenure in the White House, Zacharia reportedly remains in lockstep with Trump on certain topics — both social and political. Earlier this month, the president sat down for an interview on CBS’s "60 Minutes," where correspondent Ross Douthat asked whether he would consider forgiving his political enemies if faced with the decision while standing at the gates of Heaven. "I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies and I always will," Trump replied. Zacharia appeared to agree with the president on the topic of forgiveness, telling The Free Press that she has found it difficult to pray for her own enemies. "I respect him for saying it," Zacharia said. "That’s how we all feel. I had friends telling me after everything that happened that I needed to be praying for my enemies, and I was like, ‘No, justice is the Lord’s, and sometimes you want to see retribution for those who have harmed you.’" REPUBLICANS NEED HISTORY LESSON ABOUT THEIR PARTY IF THEY WANT TO MOVE ON FROM DEFEAT She went on to say that she would not offer forgiveness to the alleged killer of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, adding, "Erika [Kirk] might be able to, but I can't." Zacharia’s comments regarding religion and forgiveness sparked criticism from Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff, who told Fox News Digital that her stance is surprisingly in conflict with her Christian faith. "What jumped out to me was how casually she agreed with Trump that you shouldn’t forgive or pray for your enemies," Shroff said. "Republicans talk constantly about Christian values, but apparently one of Christianity’s clearest teachings becomes negotiable when Trump has a grievance." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Shroff went on to point to Democratic Sen.-elect James Talarico’s use of religion in his successful campaign in Texas — a move that marked a significant shift surrounding the party’s appetite for religious candidates. "We saw James Talarico succeed at pointing out a lot of those double standards when it comes to faith on the right," Shroff told Fox News Digital. "So it does seem that Republicans have ceded ground on the topic of faith with all of the Trump administration and MAGA hypocrisy around it." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and Zacharia for comment.

articles.title: Trump praises Zacharia amid California state bar investigation
articles.summary: President Trump heaped praise on former White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia in a phone interview Saturday, defending her quick exit from the role earlier this fall. “I saw the way she was being treated and I said, ‘Katie, you don’t need this,’” Trump told Fox News’ Kayleigh McEnany, a former Trump press secretary. “She…
articles.body:
President Trump heaped praise on former White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia in a phone interview Saturday, defending her quick exit from the role earlier this fall.

“I saw the way she was being treated and I said, ‘Katie, you don’t need this,’” Trump told Fox News’ Kayleigh McEnany, a former Trump press secretary. “She might have been able to fight her way out of it, but why should she be put in that position?”

Zacharia was dismissed from the White House press secretary role after reports emerged that she never passed the state bar exam despite repeatedly claiming she was an attorney. The California state bar exam opened an investigation into the former press secretary after a watchdog group filed a complaint, alleging she broke state law.

Trump was not asked about and did not mention the investigation in Saturday’s interview, but blamed the media for Zacharia’s short stint in the role.

“Katie was a very good person and might have been very good, I just didn’t think that she needed to have to fight for her life like that,” Trump said. “The radical left, the fake news, they really came after her.”

Zacharia previously gave a similar reason for her departure, accusing the media of having “Trump Derangement Syndrome” in a New York Post op-ed.

“The president deserves a press corps that reports his results straight — instead of feeding the incurable Trump Derangement Syndrome that fake news keeps alive,” she wrote.

Zacharia never claimed reports that she did not pass the bar exam were fake, and she later admitted herself that she did not pass, but claimed she was an attorney anyway.

A watchdog group sent a letter to the California State Bar Association outlining the several instances in which Zacharia was described as an attorney in TV appearances, and even when Trump announced he had selected her for the role.

“She has been identified on screen as a lawyer in at least 18 Fox News appearances since March 2025, has claimed to have served as ‘outside counsel’ to the World Bank and the International Finance Corporation, and listed herself as full-time General Counsel of Fix California, a California-based nonprofit, from January 2024 to March 2025,” the group said in its release about the complaint.

California law prevents anyone not licensed by the state bar from portraying themselves as a lawyer, an offense punishable by up to one year in jail.

The state bar’s investigation was initiated earlier this month and became public this week. Zacharia’s spokesperson told the LA Times the investigation was “politically motivated.”

articles.title: Trump’s grip on GOP tested as MAGA allies head for exit
articles.summary: President Trump’s grip on the Republican Party is being seriously tested after the midterm thumping, as stalwarts of his “Make America Great Again” (MAGA) movement flee the ship. Elon Musk’s statement that he is “not MAGA,” a 180-degree turn from where he stood after Trump’s inauguration, is the most notable example. But Musk is not…
articles.body:
President Trump’s grip on the Republican Party is being seriously tested after the midterm thumping, as stalwarts of his “Make America Great Again” (MAGA) movement flee the ship.

Elon Musk’s statement that he is “not MAGA,” a 180-degree turn from where he stood after Trump’s inauguration, is the most notable example. But Musk is not alone.

Podcaster Joe Rogan, who backed Trump’s 2024 presidential bid, said last week that the president’s policies did not only “lose podcast bros” but also “most of the country.”

Meanwhile, just one day after the midterm elections, conservative host and former MAGA stalwart Tucker Carlson declared that the election marked “the end of the Trump era.”

However, it was Musk’s comments that were arguably the most striking. The tech billionaire was the single largest individual donor in the midterms, spending a whopping $446 million to back Republican candidates and groups.

Despite being one of MAGA’s most forward-facing leaders over the past two years, Musk proclaimed at the New York Times Dealbook Summit on Thursday that he is “not MAGA.”

“If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that,” he said.

Some Republicans argue that MAGA’s influencers and supporters should be looking inward to figure out why the party fell so short earlier this month.

“Republicans should be free thinkers and not puppets,” said Republican strategist Mehek Cooke. “Elon Musk, Joe Rogan and any commentator asking why voters should vote Republican again are absolutely right to ask.”

“MAGA is a movement that brought people into our party who felt Washington had stopped listening to them. We can give President Trump credit for that and have a tough conversation about where we’ve fallen short. We can do both without letting a four-letter word divide us,” she said.

Others said Musk would be wise to be careful with his criticism of MAGA, noting the movement could mount a comeback.

“MAGA is damaged by the midterms but certainly could rise again,” said Dan Eberhart, a Republican donor. “Musk should stay with the team he chose and not twist with the wind. You can’t be friends with both parties.”

Trump referred to Musk as “a friend” with “very good intentions” when asked about Musk’s comments during an interview with NBC News on Thursday. However, the president also appeared to issue a warning to Musk in the same interview, saying that allies who veer from MAGA “don’t do very well.”

Meanwhile, on their way out of Capitol Hill, departing Republican lawmakers are issuing their own warnings about the current state of the GOP.

Retiring Rep. Ryan Zinke (R-Mont.), who served as Interior secretary in Trump’s first administration, told “The Hill” on NewsNation on Thursday that many GOP lawmakers have started to move on from Trump.

“They’re moving on, but no doubt the president took a little pain off of them,” Zinke said, adding that Trump “is still a force of nature.”

Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.), who lost her reelection bid, said in an interview with The Associated Press this week that the election “could be a referendum” on Trump, Congress and the Republican Party.

Republicans suffered their biggest midterm election loss in decades, where Democrats emerged with 56 seats in the Senate and at least 257 seats in the House. The Republican losses occurred in statewide races as well, with Democrats securing victories in gubernatorial and state legislative contests across the country.

Cooke argued Congress ultimately bears at least some responsibility for the shellacking.

“Republican lawmakers need to show what they’ve delivered, too. Where is the lasting legislation that makes life more affordable for working families?” Cooke said.

Recent polling shows MAGA’s supporters are well aware of the problems the movement faced on Election Day. A Politico poll released last week found that 45 percent of self-identified MAGA supporters said the movement was a loser in the midterms, while 59 percent of overall respondents said the same.

Thirty-four percent of MAGA supporters said Trump was the loser in the election, while 62 percent of respondents overall said the same.

Andrew Kolvet, spokesperson for the conservative advocacy group Turning Point USA, urged MAGA to “get back to what won us a trifecta in 2024.”

“Populist economic nationalism, sovereignty and immigration, rule of law, transparency, anti-woke and pro-common sense, and focusing on domestic renewal and revival over foreign entanglements,” Kolvet said.

“Less bluster, more results. We need to rebuild credibility, and that comes by doubling down, not jettisoning, the ideas that our base voted for in 2024,” he continued.

The future of MAGA could end up being defined in 2028, when Republicans will formally nominate a successor to Trump.

Eberhart warned that Trump would need to endorse a successor sooner rather than later to ensure MAGA remains the dominant faction of the GOP.

“If Trump waits too long to endorse for 2028, he puts the MAGA movement in jeopardy of being eclipsed by a different faction,” he said.

articles.title: Hubbard leads Foxx by 330 votes after recount
articles.summary: Democrat Chuck Hubbard remains in the lead over incumbent Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-N.C.) after a nearly finalized recount changed only one vote. Hubbard leads by 330 votes in the race for North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District. Decision Desk HQ, The Hill’s nonpartisan election results partner, has not projected a winner in the race. Foxx had…
articles.body:
Democrat Chuck Hubbard remains in the lead over incumbent Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-N.C.) after a nearly finalized recount changed only one vote.

Hubbard leads by 330 votes in the race for North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District. Decision Desk HQ, The Hill’s nonpartisan election results partner, has not projected a winner in the race.

Foxx had previously requested the recount, citing state law allowing that candidates request one when the margin of victory is under 1 percent. The sitting lawmaker does not appear to have commented on the state of the race since shortly after Election Day, when she said she would let the counting process continue.

“The continuing process, our laws, and faithful election administration will determine the election in the 5th District – and nothing else,” she wrote on social platform X.

Hubbard shared a photo to X of him attending new member orientation in Washington, which candidates are usually permitted to do in uncalled races. He does not appear to have otherwise commented on the counting process.

If Hubbard does pull off a win in the 5th district, it would be a major upset and yet another seat North Carolina Republicans lost this year. On the heels of a strong performance by Sen.-elect Roy Cooper (D), who won by 20 points, Democrats in the Tar Heel State flipped six congressional seats and came within less than 2 points in the remaining three GOP-held districts.

The 5th district would be the seventh pickup for Democrats despite a map drawn to strongly disadvantage the party.

After the 2024 election, North Carolina Republicans already held 10 congressional seats to Democrats’ four but redrew the maps mid-decade to target Rep. Don Davis (D) in the 1st Congressional District. Not only did Davis survive the challenge, but the GOP lost several additional seats .

Foxx, a 10-term incumbent first elected in 2004, has already filed for a comeback bid in 2028, when she will be 85.

articles.title: Retired FBI agent warns NCIC breach could threaten police safety during traffic stops
articles.summary: Retired FBI agent Jason Pack warns a hack of the National Crime Information Center could endanger officers at traffic stops if records were altered.
articles.body: A retired FBI supervisory special agent warned Saturday that a cyber intrusion into the bureau's National Crime Information Center (NCIC) could endanger police officers during traffic stops if hackers altered records inside the database. Jason Pack, a former FBI supervisory special agent who worked in cybercrime and public information, told Fox News Digital that the bureau's incident response team must quickly determine whether data was manipulated inside the system, which feeds criminal records to patrol cars nationwide. "What they worry about is if any of this data has changed, then it might affect officers' safety on the side of the road," Pack said, noting there is no indication yet that any records were altered or that the system is experiencing an outage. FBI PROBES SECOND CYBERATTACK IN MONTHS AS HACKERS BREACH KEY CRIME DATABASE, SOURCES SAY Three sources familiar with the matter told Fox News that hackers breached the NCIC, marking the second cyberattack against the bureau in months. The FBI is investigating how the intruders gained entry and whether any information was compromised. In an interview with Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany on Saturday morning, President Donald Trump said he had "just heard" about the intrusion, adding, "I will say that it’s not good. I don’t like that." Pack described the NCIC as "America's computer for law enforcement," explaining that roughly 56 state terminals feed data out to hundreds of thousands of patrol car computers, so officers can check warrants, criminal histories, missing children, gang members and suspected terrorists. FBI SAYS SOURCE OF ITS JOBS PORTAL BREACH STILL UNKNOWN AS HACKERS ALLEGE EMPLOYEE DATA COMPROMISED While the database does not hold classified intelligence or sensitive FBI investigative case files, Pack said it stores personally identifiable information, including names, dates of birth and Social Security numbers. Investigators will examine IP logs and metadata to determine whether attackers exploited a compromised password among the system's more than 100,000 users, breached a state terminal or infiltrated through a third-party vendor, Pack said, adding that cyberattacks have accelerated to "machine speed" as criminals increasingly use artificial intelligence to probe for vulnerabilities. "You have this cat and mouse game where cybersecurity experts are trying to patch the vulnerabilities that they find. They're looking for their own vulnerabilities at the same time, they have to play defense against the criminals who are out there trying to steal information or do harm to our systems. I think we're just seeing now this speed of these intrusions ramp up a lot," Pack said. TECH OUTAGE CASCADE EXPOSES US VULNERABILITIES TO FOREIGN CYBER THREATS The intrusion follows a September cyberattack in which the extortion group ShinyHunters breached an FBI job portal website and claimed to steal personal records belonging to bureau employees. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The latest incident also comes as a Government Accountability Office (GAO) report found 17 of 22 government agencies were not in compliance with federal cybersecurity regulations. The FBI did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the NCIC breach. Fox News Digital's James Cirrone and Greg Norman-Diamond, and Fox News' David Spunt contributed to this report.

Jeffries’s nomination was one of many significant firsts in the lower chamber. House Democrats also elected Rep. Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) as the first woman for…
articles.body:
House Democrats nominated Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) this week for the Speakership, teeing up what would mark his historic appointment as the first Black lawmaker to lead the legislative chamber.

Jeffries’s nomination was one of many significant firsts in the lower chamber. House Democrats also elected Rep. Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) as the first woman for majority leader, Rep. Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.) as the first Hispanic lawmaker for majority whip and Rep. Sarah McBride (D-Del.) — whose appointment as a committee chair made her the first transgender person elevated to House leadership.

Jeffries is scheduled to appear on CBS News’s “Face the Nation” this Sunday to discuss the Democratic agenda in the next Congress.

In the Senate, Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) is facing a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) to lead Democrats in the majority. Van Hollen has the support of progressive lawmakers who have cited discontent with Schumer’s leadership and called for generational change.

Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders (Vt.), who caucuses with Democrats, told MS NOW’s Chris Hayes this week he was working to ramp up support for the Maryland Democrat in this leadership election. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) also backed Van Hollen this week, bringing his total count of supporters to at least six votes.

“I like Chuck, but I think there has not been the sense of urgency that we have needed to address the enormous, enormous crises facing working families in this country,” Sanders said Tuesday.

Van Hollen will join NBC News’s “Meet the Press” Sunday.

Democrats in both chambers have vowed to use their oversight powers to investigate President Trump and members of his administration for a collection of alleged violations. The White House appeared to respond to these threats through an executive order seeking to limit Congress’s ability to request information from federal agencies — citing executive privilege.

Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), the ranking member on the House Judiciary Committee, sent letters to several federal agencies Thursday to warn them against using Signal or other auto-deleting messaging apps, saying it violates the law and could hinder oversight probes.

Raskin will appear on CNN’s “State of the Union” this Sunday.

Senate Republicans are continuing to push forward their agenda during the lame duck period, including advancing judicial nominees and approving a major infrastructure and energy bill .

Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.), who sits on the Senate Judiciary Committee, will join “Meet the Press” this Sunday.

The Pentagon’s $350 billion defense funding request hit a snag among GOP lawmakers this week. Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Ala.), who chairs the House Armed Services Committee, shot down the reconciliation ask on Wednesday, saying, “350 is not going to happen.”

Additionally, House Republicans struggled with attendance issues among lawmakers who were ousted in the midterm elections. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) urged his colleagues on Friday to show up for votes and “remain fully engaged” during the remainder of the current legislative session.

On Thursday, Trump engaged in a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at a summit in Shenzhen, China after attending an Association of Southeast Asian Nations gathering in Manila this week.

Trump warmly greeted his Russian counterpart as a “friend” during the meetup, verbiage he defended during a White House press briefing Friday.

“Who is he? He’s my friend,” Trump said while walking into the meeting room Thursday.

The meeting came amid national security concerns tied to CNN reporting that new U.S. intelligence suggested Iran was planning to detonate a chemical weapon in Washington, D.C.

The two top members of the House Intelligence Committee, Reps. Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) and Jim Himes (D-Conn.), are scheduled to appear on “Fox News Sunday.”

Senate Republicans voted down an Iran war powers resolution on Thursday, despite defections from GOP Sens. Susan Collins (Maine), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) and Rand Paul (Ky.).

Democratic Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) was the sole Democrat to vote against the measure.

Additionally, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton sought this week to calm cybersecurity concerns tied to recent outages at Microsoft, Apple, Google and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), among others.

The White House’s national cyber security director, Sean Cairncross, was let go from his role this week. A White House official told The Hill Thursday Trump supported his removal because he believed Cairncross did not have the proper cyber credentials for the job.

Clayton will join “State of the Union,” Fox News’s “Fox News Sunday” and ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday, while Microsoft President Brad Smith is set to appear on “Face the Nation.”

Fallout also continues after the Nvidia board’s decision to remove its co-founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, from his top post at the company following revelations about his infidelity, including with an alleged Chinese spy.

Last week, California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) issued subpoenas to the tech company, citing reports that it sold advanced AI computer chips to China. Reuters reported Friday that the Security Exchange Commission had opened a probe into the semiconductor company’s account, further tanking its stock, according to two sources briefed on the matter.

“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” Bonta said in a press release.

articles.title: Trump orders federal contractors to check with White House before responding to Congress
articles.summary: NEW YORK — President Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to a new executive order.
articles.body: NEW YORK — President Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to a new executive order. The companies must also coordinate with the White House and U.S. agencies on “appropriate responses” to any such requests, the order issued late Friday says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended. The order is the Republican administration’s latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets, noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Trump’s family, particularly at the Pentagon. White House officials have already begun taking steps to exert more control over how agencies and officials respond to congressional requests, anticipating there will be a flood of investigations initiated by Democrats. Trump’s counsel, Will Scharf, told federal agencies Monday that they must seek approval from his office and the White House’s Office of Legislative Affairs before agreeing to appear before Congress. Scharf also suggested in a recent letter to Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, that some congressional investigations may amount to “blatant criminality.” Garcia sent letters this week directing members of Trump’s family and top administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, noting in a letter to Democratic lawmakers that they are not yet in the majority and cannot compel compliance. Responding to the new executive order, Garcia said it was part of the administration’s “blatant attack on Congress’ constitutional right to conduct oversight.” He said that despite efforts to impede investigations, “we’re just getting started.” In a fact sheet, the White House framed the new requirements as “protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach,” arguing that some congressional leaders have tried to intrude on executive branch privileges by “harassing private companies that contract with the federal government.” Presidents of both parties have long used executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries, but the claims can set up messy, protracted legal fights as parties dispute whether it applies. Executive privilege allows the president to keep information from the courts, Congress and the public to protect the confidentiality of White House deliberations, but the protection is far from absolute. The latest executive order applies to all contractors and subcontractors, a universe of tens of thousands of businesses.

articles.title: Câmara deve votar projeto de ajuste fiscal nesta segunda | G1
articles.standfirst: Relator manteve o mesmo texto aprovado pelo Senado. Mauro Benevides disse que evitaria mudanças para aprovação do texto ser acelerada; ajuste economiza R$ 50 bilhões em 2027.
articles.summary: Relator manteve o mesmo texto aprovado pelo Senado. Mauro Benevides disse que evitaria mudanças para aprovação do texto ser acelerada; ajuste economiza R$ 50 bilhões em 2027.
articles.body:
A Câmara dos Deputados deve votar nesta segunda-feira (23) a proposta de ajuste fiscal do governo. O relator da proposta, deputado Mauro Benevides (União Brasil-CE), manteve o mesmo texto aprovado pelo Senado na semana passada.

Normalmente, os deputados não costumam fazer votações às segundas, mas o presidente da Câmara, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), decidiu acelerar a votação . A ausência de mudanças no parecer de Benevides tem o mesmo motivo.

O deputado afirma que uma aprovação rápida do ajuste fiscal de Lula deve mandar uma boa sinalização sobre a economia brasileira para o mercado e para a sociedade.

Com a proposta, o governo pretende conter o crescimento das despesas públicas e aumentar a arrecadação. O objetivo, de acordo com o governo, é estabilizar a dívida pública, preservando políticas sociais.

Depois da passagem pelo Senado, o projeto encabeçado pelo ministro do Planejamento, Bruno Moretti, manteve suas principais medidas. Entre elas, estão:

um limite de 2% para o crescimento de gastos em anos nos quais contingenciamento seja necessário; e

a efetivação de uma defesa antiga do governo: um novo corte linear de 10% em benefícios que o governo dá aos mais diferentes setores da economia.

O relator do texto no Senado, Eduardo Braga (MDB-AM), projetou um impacto nas contas públicas de R$ 50 bilhões em 2027.

Plenário da Câmara dos Deputados — Foto: Divulgação / Câmara dos Deputados

"Na verdade, não houve reforma fiscal, houve um ajuste para que o orçamento da União permita que a gente tenha governança sobre o orçamento no ano que vem. Se a gente não tiver governança, a gente não consegue governar", afirmou Lula sobre a proposta que ainda será analisada pela Câmara.

O presidente voltou a dizer que não fará cortes em programas sociais e fez críticas a agentes do mercado financeiro contrários à política econômica do seu governo.

🔎 Atualmente, empresas que possuem créditos tributários podem deixar de pagar outros impostos, mesmo que sejam de origem diferente dos que deram direito ao crédito.

Pelo projeto, o governo poderá estabelecer restrições a essas compensações, com percentuais diferenciados conforme o valor. A medida poderá ser adotada em momentos nos quais o governo entre em contenção de gastos.

Em manifestações separadas, divulgadas em 12 de novembro, CNI, Fiesp e a Federação das Indústrias do Estado de Minas Gerais (Fiemg) sustentaram que os grandes empresários arcarão com a maior parte do custo do ajuste.

Na prática, a restrição pode aumentar a arrecadação em dinheiro no curto prazo, porque parte dos tributos que seria pago com créditos terá de ser efetivamente paga, com dinheiro, pelas empresas.
